Two Stage Fixed Width Confidence Interval for a Distribution Free Mean

Source: R/ts_fwd_dfr_mean.R
ts_fwd_dfr_mean.Rd

Evaluates the two stage procedure for a confidence interval of fixed width for a population mean \(\mu\) when no distribution is assumed (only a finite variance). The first stage (pilot_data) fixes the total sample size; the second stage (additional_data) completes it. The interval is \(\bar{X}_N \pm d\), where d is the half width (the margin of error) and \(\bar{X}_N\) is the mean of all observations from both stages.

Usage

ts_fwd_dfr_mean(
  pilot_data,
  additional_data = NULL,
  d,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

Arguments

pilot_data

Numeric vector of the first stage observations, at least two. The whole first stage must be supplied at every call, because it alone determines the total sample size.

additional_data

Numeric vector of the second stage observations collected so far, or NULL (the default) when none have been collected.

d

The half width of the confidence interval (the margin of error), in the units of the data. A single positive number. The full width is \(2d\).

conf_level

The nominal confidence level, strictly between 0 and 1. Default 0.95. The level is asymptotic; see Details for the size of the shortfall.

na.rm

Logical. If TRUE (the default), missing values are removed from both stages before anything is computed; if FALSE, a missing value is an error.

Value

An object of class c("smsd_check", "data.frame") (see smsd_check_methods for its print(), summary(), and tidy() methods) with columns term and value and five rows:

lower_limit

\(\bar{X} - d\), with \(\bar{X}\) the mean of all observations supplied.

mean

\(\bar{X}\), the estimate of \(\mu\).

upper_limit

\(\bar{X} + d\).

optimal_n

The total sample size \(N\) fixed by the first stage.

current_n

The number of observations supplied, both stages together.

Attributes: is_satisfied (TRUE once current_n is at least optimal_n), current_n, criterion_n (equal to optimal_n), conf_level, width (the full width \(2d\)), method, and notes (always empty for this function). There is no variance_unusable attribute: a first stage whose variance cannot be estimated is an error (see Details).

Details

With \(m\) first stage observations and their sample variance \(S_m^2\), the total sample size is $$N = \max\{m,\ \lceil z_{\alpha/2}^2 \, S_m^2 / d^2 \rceil\},$$ where \(z_{\alpha/2}\) is the upper \(\alpha/2\) point of the standard normal distribution and \(\alpha = 1 - \) conf_level. If \(N = m\) the first stage is enough; otherwise \(N - m\) further observations are collected, once. \(N\) depends on the first stage alone. The row optimal_n is this total \(N\), not the number still to collect.

The confidence level is asymptotic, and the shortfall can be large. The rule plugs the first stage variance into the known variance sample size \(C = z_{\alpha/2}^2 \sigma^2 / d^2\) with no allowance for having estimated it. Once \(C\) is more than about 1.2 times the first stage, the realized coverage is therefore below the nominal level, and it approaches that level only as the first stage grows. (The figure 1.2 is for normal data, a first stage of 30, and a nominal 0.95; it is between about 1.1 and 1.3 for first stages of 5 to 200 and nominal levels of 0.90 to 0.99. When the first stage is nearly as large as \(C\), or larger, more observations are taken than the target calls for and coverage is at or above nominal.) For normal data and a narrow target the coverage is \(P(|t_{m-1}| \le z_{\alpha/2})\): at a nominal 0.95, 0.918 for a first stage of 10, 0.940 for 30, and 0.947 for 100. For skewed data it is lower. With the first stage that ts_fwd_dfr_mean_pilot returns by default (30 observations unless the target is very narrow), the coverage at a nominal 0.95 for populations with standard deviation 2 is:

Half width d10.50.20.1
Known variance sample size \(C\)15.461.53841537
Normal data0.9940.9420.9410.940
Exponential data (skewness 2)0.9960.9190.9150.917
Lognormal data (skewness 4)0.9980.9280.8740.876

The normal row is exact; the other rows are from 20,000 simulated studies per cell (standard error at most 0.0023). At d = 1 the first stage of 30 already exceeds the sample size needed, which is why coverage there is above nominal. Larger first stages help slowly: with 100 first stage observations the narrow target coverages are 0.947 (normal), 0.936 (exponential), and 0.918 (lognormal). A first stage of only two observations gives 0.78 for normal data at d = 1.

If the data can be taken as normal, use ts_fwd_norm_mean instead: Stein's procedure replaces \(z_{\alpha/2}\) by a t quantile and its coverage is exact for any first stage size. If they cannot, consider the purely sequential seq_fwd_dfr_mean, which keeps updating the variance estimate as observations arrive (its level is asymptotic too). This two stage rule is for studies in which only one further round of data collection is possible; give it as large a first stage as the study allows.

The interval rows are reported at every call so that progress can be followed, but the interval carries even its asymptotic confidence level only when the stopping rule is met, that is, when the current sample size has reached optimal_n.

A first stage with no variation is an error. If every first stage observation is equal, or equal up to rounding error (a range of no more than \(10^{-10}\) times the largest absolute value, the rule used throughout the package), the first stage variance cannot be estimated and the function stops with an error that says what to do. The purely sequential functions report such data as a stopping rule that is not yet met, with the attribute variance_unusable; here that would mislead, because the total sample size is fixed by the first stage alone, so no later observation could turn a rule reported as not met into one that is met. Data whose real variation is that small beside their size (times recorded in seconds since 1970 that differ by hundredths of a second, for example) should have a common value subtracted from both stages first; the total sample size does not depend on it.

References

Mukhopadhyay, N., & de Silva, B. M. (2009). Sequential methods and their applications. Chapman & Hall/CRC. ISBN:9780367386535

See also

ts_fwd_dfr_mean_pilot for the first stage size; ts_fwd_norm_mean for the exact procedure under normality; seq_fwd_dfr_mean for the purely sequential procedure.

Other ts_fwd_dfr_mean: ts_fwd_dfr_mean_pilot()

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu, Bhargab Chattopadhyay bhargab@iiitvadodara.ac.in

Examples

# An HR analyst wants mean weekly hours of unpaid overtime to within
# half an hour, with a nominal 95% confidence level; the hours are
# right skewed, so normality is not assumed.
set.seed(113)
m <- ts_fwd_dfr_mean_pilot(d = 0.5, conf_level = 0.95)
first_stage <- rgamma(m, shape = 2, rate = 0.5)
check <- ts_fwd_dfr_mean(first_stage, d = 0.5)
check
#> Sequential check (two stage fixed width interval (distribution free mean))
#> 
#>   Current n       : 30
#>   Criterion n     : 91
#>   Target width    : 1
#>   Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#>   lower_limit       : 2.652349
#>   mean              : 3.152349
#>   upper_limit       : 3.652349
#>   optimal_n         : 91
#>   current_n         : 30
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: FALSE

# The first stage fixed the total sample size; collect the remainder.
n_more <- attr(check, "criterion_n") - attr(check, "current_n")
second_stage <- rgamma(n_more, shape = 2, rate = 0.5)
ts_fwd_dfr_mean(first_stage, second_stage, d = 0.5)
#> Sequential check (two stage fixed width interval (distribution free mean))
#> 
#>   Current n       : 91
#>   Criterion n     : 91
#>   Target width    : 1
#>   Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#>   lower_limit       : 2.986092
#>   mean              : 3.486092
#>   upper_limit       : 3.986092
#>   optimal_n         : 91
#>   current_n         : 91
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: TRUE
